claims.text: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction can be used to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behavior of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy.
HTXRD enables time-resolved identification of oxide phase formation and phase transformations during oxidation.
HTXRD directly assesses phase stability during oxidation.
HTXRD provides a more detailed understanding of transformation kinetics than post-mortem analyses.
The initial CrMnFeCoNi alloy has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
CrMnFeCoNi can be studied during high-temperature oxidation in both vacuum and air environments.
The relevant oxidation temperature range is approximately 800–1200 °C.
Oxidation produces surface oxide phases, including halite and spinel oxides.
The oxide-phase assemblage evolves with oxidation time and temperature.
At elevated temperature, oxygen preferentially oxidizes Mn in CrMnFeCoNi.
Preferential oxidation of Mn leads to nucleation and growth of oxide phases.
HTXRD can link the time- and temperature-dependent evolution of oxide phases to oxidation kinetics and phase stability.
Oxidation will produce time-dependent diffraction features corresponding to emerging oxide phases.
HTXRD may reveal phase transformations in the underlying alloy lattice during oxidation.
Traditional post-mortem analysis cannot capture transient phase transformations during high-temperature oxidation.
The method is specifically validated for other HEAs whose oxidation behavior resembles that of CrMnFeCoNi.
Applicability of the method to other alloys and more extreme conditions remains to be investigated.
The quantitative correspondence between HTXRD observations and CALPHAD predictions requires further validation.
The influence of oxidation kinetics on phase stability has not been fully quantified.

contradictions.description: The uncertainty field states that CALPHAD correspondence itself requires validation, whereas the falsification rule partly treats inconsistency with CALPHAD and post-mortem results as grounds for rejecting HTXRD effectiveness. Disagreement with an acknowledged-to-be-uncertain model is not by itself decisive evidence that HTXRD failed.
